identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: The Dwarkadhish temple, known as the Jagat Mandir, is revered as the shrine of Krishna in his aspect as lord of Dwarka, the city tradition holds he ruled. Gujarat Tourism places Dwarka among the Char Dham alongside Badrinath, Puri and Rameshwaram, and the site also carries a memorial to Adi Shankara's visit. Pilgrims conventionally enter by the Swarga Dwar and leave by the Moksha Dwar.

governance.establishedEra: Ancient; multiple renovations · Current structure 15th-16th century

narrative.summaryIntro:
Dwarkadhish Temple, located in the ancient city of Dwarka in Gujarat, is one of the four cardinal pilgrimage sites (Char Dham) and is dedicated to Lord Krishna. The temple is believed to be built on the site where Krishna ruled his kingdom and is a major center of Vaishnavite worship. The present structure stands at a height of approximately 51.5 meters with elaborate stone carvings.

According to Hindu tradition, Dwarka was the capital of Krishna's kingdom and remains a sacred pilgrimage destination. The temple features intricate architectural details characteristic of Gujarat's temple-building tradition. It is revered as one of the oldest and most important Krishna temples in India, attracting devotees year-round.
narrative.documentedHistory:
The Devbhumi Dwarka district administration records two accounts of the temple's age side by side: the traditional attribution to Vajranabh, Krishna's great-grandson, more than 2500 years ago, and the opinion of the Department of Archaeology that the structure is about 1200 years old. Gujarat Tourism records that the temple was destroyed by Mahmud Begada in 1472 and rebuilt over the 15th and 16th centuries, which is also when the present enlargement is dated.

The main shrine sits on Gomti creek and is known as the Jagat Mandir, the universal shrine, or trilok sundar. It is built of soft limestone and comprises a sanctum, a vestibule and a rectangular hall with porches on three sides. Wikipedia describes it as a five-storeyed building carried on 72 pillars, roughly 29 m east to west by 23 m north to south. The shikhar is given as 43 m high by both the district administration and Gujarat Tourism, though Wikipedia states 78 m; the flag above it is made from 52 yards of cloth and is said to be visible from 10 km away, and is changed several times daily.

The complex has two named gateways. The district administration describes the swarga dwar as the gate by which pilgrims enter and the moksha dwar as the gate by which they leave; Wikipedia places the Moksha Dwara on the north and the Swarga Dwara on the south, with a flight of 56 steps descending from it to the ghats of the Gomati. A memorial within the temple commemorates Adi Shankara's visit, and the Dvaraka Pitha he is said to have founded stands nearby.

visitingInfo.nearestBusStation: Connected by highways from major cities
visitingInfo.entryRules: Pilgrims enter by the swarga dwar and exit by the moksha dwar. The Sudama Setu footbridge across the Gomti creek is open 7:00 AM-1:00 PM and 4:00-7:30 PM.
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Neither the district administration nor Gujarat Tourism publishes a temple telephone number; confirm darshan and aarti timings with the temple administration on arrival, or through the Devbhumi Dwarka district office directory.

shrines.locationDescription: One of the complex's two named gateways. The district administration describes it as the gate by which pilgrims enter; Wikipedia places it on the south side, opening onto 56 steps down to the Gomati ghats.
The complex's other named gateway. The district administration describes it as the exit; Wikipedia places it as the northern entrance.
A memorial within the temple marking Adi Shankara's visit to the shrine.

festivals.significance: Gujarat Tourism notes that Janmashtami, the birth of Krishna, is celebrated grandly at Dwarka and names it as one of the best times to visit.
festivals.visitorAdvice: Expect heavy crowds; Gujarat Tourism otherwise recommends November to February for a comfortable visit.
